title: Bosons, Fermions and Bose-Einstein Condensates

cards.b: All identical particles in nature fall into two families that behave in opposite ways: fermions refuse to share a state, bosons love to. That single difference explains why matter is solid, why lasers exist, why stars do not collapse and why liquid helium creeps up walls.

Two electrons are exactly identical, not just similar. Swap them and nothing changes. Quantum theory says the wavefunction of two identical particles either keeps its sign (bosons) or flips it (fermions) when they are swapped. If it flips, putting both in the same state would give zero: so fermions are barred from sharing. That is the Pauli principle.

Spin-half particles (electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks) are fermions. Whole-number-spin particles (photons, gluons, W and Z bosons, the Higgs) are bosons. Composite particles count: helium-4 (two protons, two neutrons, two electrons: six fermions) is a boson, helium-3 (five fermions) is a fermion. Paul Dirac named the two families after Bose and Enrico Fermi.

In 1924 S.N. Bose derived Planck's law by counting identical light quanta. Einstein extended it to atoms (1924-25) and saw a strange consequence: cool enough, a gas of bosons would all fall into the lowest state. In 1926 Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac separately gave the rules for particles that obey exclusion.

cards.h: A matter wave of its own
cards.b: At extremely low temperatures, boson atoms pile into one quantum state and act as one giant matter wave. It was first made in 1995 by Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman (JILA, rubidium atoms, about 170 billionths of a kelvin above absolute zero) and by Wolfgang Ketterle (MIT, sodium). All three shared the 2001 Nobel Prize. This was 70 years after the prediction.

• Superfluid helium-4 flows without friction below 2.17 K (Kapitza; Allen and Misener, 1937-38).
  • Superconductors: electrons pair up into boson-like pairs (Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, 1957).
  • Lasers: photons crowd into one mode.
  • White dwarfs and neutron stars: fermion crowding resists gravity.

When a star burns out, electrons squeezed together must occupy higher and higher states, which creates "degeneracy pressure", not from heat. This holds up white dwarfs. In 1930 the young Indian physicist S. Chandrasekhar, on a ship to England, calculated that above about 1.4 solar masses this pressure fails and a white dwarf must collapse. The Chandrasekhar limit explains supernovae of Type Ia. He shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

• "Bosons are force particles and fermions are matter." A useful first rule, but composite bosons (helium-4) are matter too.
  • "A condensate is a solid." It is an ultracold gas, not frozen.
  • "Fermions repel each other by a force." It is a counting rule, not a push.

S.N. Bose gave his name to bosons and to Bose-Einstein statistics; he was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1954. S. Chandrasekhar (born in Lahore, 1910) made the fermion argument for stars. India's labs also work with ultracold atoms, for example at the Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru, and these skills feed quantum sensing and computing under the National Quantum Mission.

• Fermions (half-integer spin) cannot share a state; bosons can.
  • BEC: bosons pile into one state; made in 1995, Nobel 2001.
  • Fermion crowding supports white dwarfs up to 1.4 solar masses (Chandrasekhar).

Think about it

  1. Why is helium-4 a boson but helium-3 a fermion?
  2. How does the Pauli principle stop a white dwarf from collapsing?
